passages.passageHtml: Grammar and usage questions focusing on subject-verb agreement, pronoun agreement, verb tense, and standard English usage.

questions.questionHtml: Choose the sentence that is written correctly.

options.A: The basket of fresh apples smell delicious, but some of it is overripe.
options.B: The basket of fresh apples smells delicious, but some of them are overripe.
options.C: The basket of fresh apples smell delicious, but some of them is overripe.
options.D: The basket of fresh apples smells delicious, but some of it are overripe.

questions.explanationHtml: The subject "basket" is singular → requires "smells" (eliminates A and C). "Some of them" refers to individual apples → plural "are" (correct in B). D has "some of it ... are" - "it" is singular but "are" is plural, so incorrect.

questions.questionHtml:
Choose the phrase that correctly completes the sentence.
Everyone on the team finished practice drills before the coach arrived.
questions.explanationHtml: "Everyone" is an indefinite singular pronoun → traditionally paired with "his or her" on the GED. B ("their") is common in speech but often marked incorrect on this test. C ("its") is for objects/animals, not people. D ("there") indicates location.

questions.questionHtml:
Choose the word pair that correctly completes the sentence.
The new policy will all employees, for those on medical leave.
questions.explanationHtml: First blank needs a verb meaning "to influence" → "affect" (not "effect"). Second blank means "excluding" → "except" (not "accept"). A and B each have one correct and one incorrect word; D has both wrong.

questions.questionHtml: Choose the sentence that is written in standard English.

options.A: We should of left earlier, but the dog needed walked.
options.B: We should have left earlier, but the dog needed walking.
options.C: We should of left earlier, but the dog needed to be walked.
options.D: We should have left earlier, but the dog needed walked.

questions.explanationHtml: "Should have" (not "should of") eliminates A and C. "Needed walked" (as in "needed to be walked") is nonstandard English - eliminates D. "Needed walking" (standard) or "needed to be walked" are both acceptable; only B fits with correct "should have."

options.A: There is several reasons for the delay, but the main one are the weather.
options.B: There are several reasons for the delay, but the main one is the weather.
options.C: There is several reasons for the delay, but the main one is the weather.
options.D: There are several reasons for the delay, but the main one are the weather.

questions.explanationHtml: "Several reasons" is plural → "there are" (not "there is") - eliminates A and C. "The main one" is singular → "is" (not "are") - eliminates A and D. B has both verbs correct.

questions.questionHtml: Choose the sentence that is written correctly.

options.A: In the garage is stored the old tools that my father use to fix cars.
options.B: In the garage are stored the old tools that my father used to fix cars.
options.C: In the garage is stored the old tools that my father used to fix cars.
options.D: In the garage are stored the old tools that my father use to fix cars.

questions.explanationHtml:
Explanation of each option:

A is incorrect: The subject “tools” is plural, so the verb should be “are stored,” not “is stored.” Also, “use” should be past tense “used.”

B is correct: “Tools” (plural) takes “are stored.” The past tense “used to fix” correctly indicates a past habit.

C is incorrect: “Is stored” does not agree with the plural subject “tools.”

D is incorrect: Although “are stored” is correct, “use” should be “used” to maintain past tense consistency.

questions.questionHtml:
Choose the phrase that correctly completes the sentence.
Either Maria or the supervisors will submit _____ report by Friday.
questions.explanationHtml:
Explanation of each option:

A is correct: With “either…or,” the pronoun agrees with the closer subject. “Supervisors” (plural) is closer, so the plural pronoun “their” is correct.

B is incorrect: “Her” is singular and feminine, but the closer subject is plural, and gender is not specified for “supervisors.”

C is incorrect: “Its” is used for things or animals, not for people.

D is incorrect: “His or her” is singular, but the closer subject “supervisors” is plural, requiring a plural pronoun.

questions.questionHtml:
Choose the word pair that correctly completes the sentence.
After he _____ the book on the table, he _____ three hours doing nothing.
questions.explanationHtml:
Explanation of each option:

A is incorrect: “Laid” is correct for placing an object, but “past” is not a verb; “passed” is needed for spending time.

B is incorrect: “Lay” (past of “lie” – to recline) does not take an object; “the book” requires “laid.” “Passed” is correct, but the first word is wrong.

C is correct: “Laid” is the past tense of “lay” (to put something down) and takes the object “book.” “Passed” is the past tense of “pass” (to spend time).

D is incorrect: “Lay” is wrong for placing an object, and “past” is not a verb.

questions.questionHtml: Choose the sentence that is written in standard English.

options.A: He didn't have no choice but to lay down for a while.
options.B: He didn't have any choice but to lie down for a while.
options.C: He hadn't no choice but to lay down for a while.
options.D: He didn't have any choice but to lay down for a while.

questions.explanationHtml:
Explanation of each option:

A is incorrect: Double negative “didn’t have no” is nonstandard. Also “lay down” requires an object; “lie down” is correct for reclining.

B is correct: No double negative (“didn’t have any”). “Lie down” (no object) is the correct verb for a person reclining.

C is incorrect: “Hadn’t no” is a double negative. Also “lay down” is incorrect.

D is incorrect: Although “didn’t have any” fixes the double negative, “lay down” is still wrong; it should be “lie down.”

options.A: One of the students who was late have to see the principal.
options.B: One of the students who were late has to see the principal.
options.C: One of the students who was late has to see the principal.
options.D: One of the students who were late have to see the principal.

questions.explanationHtml:
Explanation of each option:

A is incorrect: The relative clause “who was late” refers to “students” (plural) and should use “were.” Also the main verb “have” does not agree with singular subject “One.”

B is correct: “Who were late” agrees with plural “students.” The main subject “One” (singular) takes the singular verb “has.”

C is incorrect: “Who was late” is singular, but it refers to “students” (plural). The relative pronoun “who” takes its number from the antecedent “students.”

D is incorrect: “Have” does not agree with singular subject “One.”

questions.questionHtml: Choose the sentence that is written correctly.

options.A: In the drawer is the keys that unlocks the front door.
options.B: In the drawer are the keys that unlock the front door.
options.C: In the drawer is the keys that unlock the front door.
options.D: In the drawer are the keys that unlocks the front door.

questions.explanationHtml: Subject "keys" (plural) → verb "are" (eliminates A and C). Relative clause "that unlock" - plural antecedent "keys" → plural verb "unlock" (eliminates D, which has "unlocks"). A has both singular errors; C has "is" wrong but "unlock" right; D has "are" right but "unlocks" wrong.

questions.questionHtml:
Choose the phrase that correctly completes the sentence.

The teacher gave the award to both you and _____, and we had to congratulate _____.
questions.explanationHtml: Object of preposition "to" → object pronoun "me" (eliminates A and C, which use "I"). Reflexive pronoun for "we" → "ourselves" (eliminates A and D, which use nonstandard "ourself"). B has both correct.

questions.questionHtml:
Choose the word pair that correctly completes the sentence.

She would rather work late _____ go home, _____ for emergency situations.
questions.explanationHtml: Comparative "rather ... than" (not "then") - eliminates A and C. "Except" (excluding) vs. "accept" (receive) - sentence means "except for emergencies" - eliminates D. B has both correct.

options.A: The jury has reached their verdict after three days of deliberation.
options.B: The jury have reached its verdict after three days of deliberation.
options.C: The jury has reached its verdict after three days of deliberation.
options.D: The jury have reached their verdict after three days of deliberation.

questions.explanationHtml: Collective noun "jury" as a single unit in American English → singular verb "has" (eliminates B and D, which use "have"). Singular pronoun "its" (not "their") - eliminates A (which has "has ... their" - inconsistent). C has both singular.

questions.questionHtml: Choose the sentence that is written in standard English.

options.A: He couldn't hardly see nothing through the fog.
options.B: He could hardly see anything through the fog.
options.C: He couldn't hardly see anything through the fog.
options.D: He could hardly see nothing through the fog.

questions.explanationHtml: "Hardly" is a negative adverb → using "couldn't" creates a double negative (eliminates A and C). "See nothing" with "hardly" is also a double negative (eliminates D). B uses "hardly see anything" – standard English.
